[Director 指令] [Partial Draft] 写 EMNLP 2026 论文的 data-independent 章节，DDL 无紧迫压力。

**目标**：先写不依赖 plan_001 实验数据的章节，plan_001 数据（15 模型 455 panels）预计 6 小时后出。

**需要写的章节**：
1. **Related Work**（~1 页）：覆盖 ensemble adversarial robustness (Tramèr et al. 2018)、adversarial transferability (Papernot et al. 2016-2017)、LLM-as-Judge (Zheng et al. 2023)、LLM judge biases (Wang et al. 2023)、prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023)、BFT (Lamport et al. 1982, Castro & Liskov 1999)、security weakest-link (Schneier 2000)、ensemble diversity theory (Krogh & Vedelsby 1995)。Dream 审稿反复标注"零引用"为 critical issue。
2. **Threat Model & Problem Formulation**（~0.5 页）：adaptive adversary model、majority vote formulation、K_eff 定义、η_max 定义、SDPI bound
3. **Methodology**（~1 页）：实验设计描述（15 models × 6 attacks × 2 benchmarks × panel enumeration）、MI estimation method、regression specification、random-fault simulation design

**Core claim**: 读 `paper_framing.md` 获取完整 narrative。关键：novelty positioning 是"first systematic empirical quantification in LLM-judge domain"，不是"discovering weakest-link principle"。

**引用需要验证**——所有引用必须真实存在。

**不要写的**：Results、Analysis、Discussion、Abstract、Conclusion（等 plan_001 数据）。

ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

We provide the first systematic empirical characterization showing this analogy breaks under adaptive adversaries: BFT assumes random faults, but LLM adversaries target the weakest judge. We quantify this via regime analysis — diversity's protective effect depends on individual judge robustness level and attack transferability — and expose structural barriers (diversity-capability tradeoff, Gaussian copula failure) that prior work has not measured.\\n\\n## Hook\\n\\\"Adding more diverse judges to an evaluation panel doesn't make it safer — it can make it worse.\\\"\\nWe empirically validate and quantify a predicted but unmeasured phenomenon in the LLM judge domain: the failure of diversity-based defenses under adaptive adversaries.\\n\\n## Novelty Positioning (Dream D4 fix)\\nWe do NOT claim to discover that weakest-link effects exist under adaptive adversaries — this is established in security (Schneier 2000) and adversarial ML (Tramèr et al. 2018). Our contributions are:\\n1. **First systematic empirical quantification** in the LLM-judge domain at scale (15+ models, 455 panels, 6+ attacks)\\n2. **Regime characterization**: when does diversity help vs hurt? (capability tier × attack transferability interaction)\\n3. **Structural barriers**: copula failure (10-21× MI underestimation), diversity-capability tradeoff, family label unreliability\\n4. **Actionable panel design guidance** grounded in formal analysis\\n\\n## Core Claims\\n\\n### Claim 1 (Primary): Weakest-Link Theorem\\n**Statement**: Under adaptive adversarial attacks, panel ASR is dominated by the individual robustness of the weakest panel member (η_max), with judge diversity (K_eff) providing no significant additional protection.\\n**Evidence**: Multivariate regression log(ASR) ~ log(K_eff) + log(η_max) on 20 K=3 panels × 12 conditions:\\n- η_max significant: **6/12 (BH-FDR q<0.05)**, 3/12 Bonferroni. ARC 4/6, MMLU 2/6 (sycophancy + verbosity).\\n- K_eff not significant: 11/12 conditions. Residualized K_eff (orthogonalized against η_max) confirms: only 1/12 significant (arc×sycophancy p=0.013, VIF=1.04).\\n- arc×position excluded from main analysis (VIF=10.02, severe multicollinearity).\\n- Beta regression concordance: 11/12 conditions agree with OLS.\\n**Strength**: Moderate-Strong. K_eff irrelevance confirmed NOT collinearity artifact (plan_009). ARC stronger than MMLU.\\n**Headline**: \\\"η_max significant in 6/12 conditions (BH-FDR); K_eff not significant in 11/12; residualized K_eff confirms 1/12.\\\"\\n\\n### Claim 2 (Empirical/Theoretical): Adaptive vs Random-Fault Regime Difference\\n**Statement**: Panel composition (K_eff + η_max) explains systematically more variance under random faults (R²=0.55-0.95) than under adaptive attacks (R²=0.14-0.73). Adaptive adversaries introduce strategic variance that panel composition cannot predict.\\n**Evidence**: (a) R² comparison across 12 conditions between adaptive and random-fault regimes; (b) Formal theorem: panel_ASR is monotonically increasing in η_max under majority vote with correlated judges (option b — provable, data-supported).\\n**⚠️ GO/NO-GO GATE FAILED (D011)**: Random-fault simulation showed K_eff 0/12 significant negative — same as adaptive. The original BFT contrast (\\\"K_eff helps under random faults but not adaptive\\\") CANNOT be demonstrated with current 6-model pool due to K_eff-η_max structural confound.\\n**Contingency**: plan_001 (15+ models) may break the confound. If C(15,3)=455 panels contain high-K_eff + low-η_max combinations, random-fault simulation may produce different results. If plan_001 also fails → drop to R²-only claim or remove Claim 2 entirely.\\n**Strength**: Weak (pending plan_001). R² difference is real but much weaker than original K_eff regime-distinction claim.\\n\\n### Claim 3 (Empirical): Diversity-Capability Tradeoff\\n**Statement**: In the current LLM ecosystem, maximizing panel diversity (K_eff) necessarily introduces less capable/robust models, creating a negative correlation between K_eff and min-judge-robustness (r ≈ -0.8). Diversity and security are structurally at odds.\\n**Evidence**: K_eff vs η_max correlation across 20 panels; capability-stratified analysis showing tradeoff persists within model tiers.\\n**Strength**: Strong (correlation). Capability-stratified analysis planned.\\n\\n### Claim 4 (Methodological): Family Labels ≠ Diversity\\n**Statement**: Model family labels (Qwen/Llama/Mistral) do not predict judge independence. Capability proximity is the primary driver of inter-judge correlation.\\n**Evidence**: Mann-Whitney U p=0.206, permutation p=0.427 for within vs cross-family MI.\\n**Strength**: Strong. Clean statistical test, N=15 pairs.\\n\\n### Claim 5 (Methodological): Gaussian Copula Failure\\n**Statement**: The Gaussian copula model systematically underestimates information sharing between LLM judges by 10-21× (up to 235×), invalidating copula-based independence bounds.\\n**Evidence**: MI_observed / MI_gaussian ratio across 15 pairs × 2 datasets.\\n**Strength**: Strong. Large effect size, consistent.\\n\\n### Claim 6 (Practical): Robustness-First Panel Design\\n**Statement**: Optimal panel selection is robustness-first: (1) screen for individual robustness (η ≤ threshold), then (2) maximize K_eff among qualifying judges. This dominates naive strategies (random, max-family-diversity, max-K_eff-only, strongest-K-models).\\n**Evidence**: Preliminary: min_eta_max strategy dominates 5/6 conditions. Full two-stage algorithm validation planned.\\n**Strength**: Moderate. Needs formal algorithm + expanded model pool validation.\\n\\n### Claim 7 (Empirical+Practical): Aggregation Rule Modulates Weakest-Link Effect\\n**Statement**: The weakest-link dominance (Claim 1) is specific to unweighted aggregation rules. Reliability-weighted (Bayesian) aggregation partially breaks the effect (η_max FDR-significant in only 2/12 conditions vs 5/12 under majority vote), while unanimity (threshold) voting makes diversity actively harmful (K_eff positively correlated with ASR).\\n**Evidence** (6-model, FDR-48 corrected, 5-fold CV validated):\\n- Majority: η_max **5/12** FDR sig (consistent with plan_009 FDR-12: 6/12)\\n- Weighted: η_max **6/12** FDR sig\\n- Threshold: η_max **6/12** FDR-48 sig + K_eff positive **8/12** FDR-12 sig (⚠️ FDR-48 may reduce to ~6/12; diversity harmful under unanimity; 4 conditions K_eff sig but η_max not — K_eff carries independent signal)\\n- Bayesian: η_max **2/12** FDR sig (Bonferroni 1/12 — mmlu__verbosity_bias β=+4.32, extreme effect survives)\\n- 5-fold CV confirms no information leakage: same 3 raw-significant conditions survive with near-identical p-values\\n**Mechanism details** (Reviewer verified):\\n- Bayesian: real effect reduction (4/12 conditions show η_max sign reversal, not just power loss) + low power (R²=0.22). Extreme attacks (prompt injection, verbosity bias) still break through. Weights = clean accuracy via 5-fold CV (\\\"calibrated Bayesian\\\") — robust to weight estimation procedure.\\n- Threshold: K_eff positive because unanimity requires all judges correct → independent judges less likely to all agree → attack only needs to flip any one judge. **ASR semantics differ from majority vote** (denominator = clean unanimity subset, not all samples) — must be disclosed.\\n**Strength**: Moderate-Strong (6-model). Key caveats: (1) Threshold ASR definition ≠ majority ASR definition (selection bias on denominator); (2) 6-model / 20-panel data, needs 455-panel validation.\\n**Paper narrative**: \\\"Bayesian aggregation mitigates but does not eliminate the weakest-link effect; the most severe vulnerability gaps survive reliability weighting.\\\"\\n**Reviewer anticipation**: \\\"Why not just use Bayesian?\\\" → (a) requires clean accuracy prior (not zero-knowledge), (b) adaptive attacker can target Bayesian specifically, (c) FDR-corrected 2/12 still significant — extreme attacks survive, (d) practical recommendation is defense stack (robustness-first selection + Bayesian aggregation), not aggregation alone.\\n\\n## Contribution Stack (ordered by strength)\\n1. **Weakest-link theorem** — primary empirical contribution (challenges diversity assumption)\\n2. **Diversity-capability tradeoff** — empirical contribution (shows structural barrier)\\n3. **Aggregation-dependent weakest-link** — empirical+practical contribution (scopes Theorem 1; Bayesian as partial defense; threshold as counterintuitive negative)\\n4. **Robustness-first panel design** — practical contribution (actionable guidance)\\n5. **Gaussian copula failure** — methodological contribution\\n6. **Family label unreliability** — methodological contribution\\n7. **Adaptive adversary vs random-fault R² gap** — conditional theoretical contribution (⚠️ pending plan_001 validation; if confound breaks with 15 models → promote to #2)\\n\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns\\n\\n### RC1: \\\"η_max dominating is obvious — of course weak judges make weak panels\\\"\\n**Response**: (a) Existing literature assumes diversity is sufficient (SoK reports \\\"7-model committees reduce ASR to 10-19%\\\" without controlling for individual model quality); (b) We formalize via adaptive adversary model showing WHY — not just THAT — this happens; (c) The diversity-capability tradeoff is non-obvious and has practical implications.\\n\\n### RC2: \\\"Only 6 models — too small for generalizable claims\\\"\\n**Response**: Expand to 15+ models including API models (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, Claude, Gemini) + larger open-source (70B class). Weakest-link theorem tested on C(15,3) = 455 panels.\\n\\n### RC3: \\\"Only limited attack types\\\"\\n**Response**: Expand to 6+ attack types covering prompt injection, score manipulation, sycophancy bias, verbosity bias, position bias, authority bias.\\n\\n### RC4: \\\"BFT comparison is a strawman — nobody literally claims BFT for LLM panels\\\"\\n**Response**: (a) The *implicit* assumption is BFT-like: \\\"more independent judges = more robust\\\"; (b) We make this implicit assumption explicit and show where it breaks; (c) Random-fault simulation shows panel composition R² is systematically higher (0.55-0.95) than under adaptive attacks (0.14-0.73), confirming that adaptive adversaries introduce strategic variance beyond what panel composition can predict — the distinction is real even though K_eff itself is not the differentiator.\\n\\n### RC5: \\\"Panel design algorithm is trivial — just use the strongest models\\\"\\n**Response**: (a) \\\"Strongest\\\" varies across attack types; (b) Two-stage algorithm outperforms both \\\"min η_max only\\\" and \\\"max K_eff only\\\" in capability-matched settings; (c) Algorithm provides principled threshold selection.\\n\\n### RC6: \\\"No theoretical novelty — just regression analysis\\\"\\n**Response**: (a) Adaptive adversary bound is a formal theorem; (b) Diversity-capability tradeoff formalization is novel; (c) Copula failure has implications for MI-based evaluation frameworks beyond this paper.\\n\\n### RC7: \\\"Why not just use Bayesian aggregation to fix the problem?\\\"\\n**Response**: (a) Bayesian aggregation requires clean accuracy as prior — not a zero-knowledge defense; (b) Adaptive adversary aware of Bayesian weighting can adjust strategy; (c) η_max still FDR-significant in 2/12 conditions (Bonferroni 1/12) — weakened but not eliminated, extreme vulnerability gaps survive; (d) The practical recommendation is a defense stack: robustness-first selection + reliability-weighted aggregation, not aggregation alone.\\n\\n## \\\"When Diversity Helps\\\" Section (Dream D13 fix)\\nDiversity IS beneficial in specific regimes — paper must acknowledge this to avoid misleading:\\n1. **Non-adversarial settings**: reducing position bias, verbosity bias, calibration\\n2. **Within the arc×sycophancy regime**: K_eff partial r=-0.64, VIF=1.04, beta reg p=8.5e-05. When individual vulnerability is uniformly high and low-variance (sycophancy on ARC), diversity provides genuine protection. This is the \\\"BFT-like\\\" regime where faults are approximately random.\\n3. **Practical guidance**: First ensure all judges exceed a robustness threshold, THEN maximize diversity among qualifying judges.\\n\\n## Story Arc\\n1. **Background**: Multi-judge LLM evaluation is increasingly adopted; diversity is assumed to be the key defense against manipulation (SoK, Yang, Turkmen)\\n2. **Tension**: This assumption mirrors BFT, which assumes random faults — but LLM adversaries are adaptive\\n3. **Insight**: Under adaptive adversaries, panel_ASR is dominated by η_max; diversity provides no protection because the attacker targets the weakest link\\n4. **Nuance**: Diversity DOES help in specific regimes (low η_max variance, shared-bias attacks) — the BFT analogy is valid only when individual vulnerabilities are already controlled\\n5. **Defense**: Aggregation rule matters — Bayesian weighting partially breaks weakest-link; unanimity makes diversity harmful. But no single aggregation eliminates the effect.\\n6. **Resolution**: Defense stack: robustness-first panel selection + reliability-weighted aggregation + regime-aware framework\\n\", \"total_chars\": 13573, \"truncated\": false}, \"error\": null, \"metadata\": {}}"}

> Last updated: 2026-05-22 | Reason: Dream review (2.5 all tiers) exposed structural issues; reframe novelty, fix theorem, add experiments

## Target
EMNLP 2026 (via ARR)

## Title Candidates
1. "The Diversity Trap: Why Adding More Judges Doesn't Make LLM Evaluation Safer"
2. "The Weakest Link: Individual Robustness Dominates Diversity in Multi-Judge LLM Evaluation Security"
3. "Against the Diversity Assumption: Adaptive Adversaries Break Multi-Judge LLM Evaluation Panels at the Weakest Link"

## Core Insight
Multi-judge LLM evaluation panels are widely assumed to benefit from judge diversity, analogous to Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) where redundancy protects against faults. We provide the first systematic empirical characterization showing this analogy breaks under adaptive adversaries: BFT assumes random faults, but LLM adversaries target the weakest judge. We quantify this via regime analysis — diversity's protective effect depends on individual judge robustness level and attack transferability — and expose structural barriers (diversity-capability tradeoff, Gaussian copula failure) that prior work has not measured.

## Hook
"Adding more diverse judges to an evaluation panel doesn't make it safer — it can make it worse."
We empirically validate and quantify a predicted but unmeasured phenomenon in the LLM judge domain: the failure of diversity-based defenses under adaptive adversaries.

## Novelty Positioning (Dream D4 fix)
We do NOT claim to discover that weakest-link effects exist under adaptive adversaries — this is established in security (Schneier 2000) and adversarial ML (Tramèr et al. 2018). Our contributions are:
1. **First systematic empirical quantification** in the LLM-judge domain at scale (15+ models, 455 panels, 6+ attacks)
2. **Regime characterization**: when does diversity help vs hurt? (capability tier × attack transferability interaction)
3. **Structural barriers**: copula failure (10-21× MI underestimation), diversity-capability tradeoff, family label unreliability
4. **Actionable panel design guidance** grounded in formal analysis

## Core Claims

### Claim 1 (Primary): Weakest-Link Theorem
**Statement**: Under adaptive adversarial attacks, panel ASR is dominated by the individual robustness of the weakest panel member (η_max), with judge diversity (K_eff) providing no significant additional protection.
**Evidence**: Multivariate regression log(ASR) ~ log(K_eff) + log(η_max) on 20 K=3 panels × 12 conditions:
- η_max significant: **6/12 (BH-FDR q<0.05)**, 3/12 Bonferroni. ARC 4/6, MMLU 2/6 (sycophancy + verbosity).
- K_eff not significant: 11/12 conditions. Residualized K_eff (orthogonalized against η_max) confirms: only 1/12 significant (arc×sycophancy p=0.013, VIF=1.04).
- arc×position excluded from main analysis (VIF=10.02, severe multicollinearity).
- Beta regression concordance: 11/12 conditions agree with OLS.
**Strength**: Moderate-Strong. K_eff irrelevance confirmed NOT collinearity artifact (plan_009). ARC stronger than MMLU.
**Headline**: "η_max significant in 6/12 conditions (BH-FDR); K_eff not significant in 11/12; residualized K_eff confirms 1/12."

### Claim 2 (Empirical/Theoretical): Adaptive vs Random-Fault Regime Difference
**Statement**: Panel composition (K_eff + η_max) explains systematically more variance under random faults (R²=0.55-0.95) than under adaptive attacks (R²=0.14-0.73). Adaptive adversaries introduce strategic variance that panel composition cannot predict.
**Evidence**: (a) R² comparison across 12 conditions between adaptive and random-fault regimes; (b) Formal theorem: panel_ASR is monotonically increasing in η_max under majority vote with correlated judges (option b — provable, data-supported).
**⚠️ GO/NO-GO GATE FAILED (D011)**: Random-fault simulation showed K_eff 0/12 significant negative — same as adaptive. The original BFT contrast ("K_eff helps under random faults but not adaptive") CANNOT be demonstrated with current 6-model pool due to K_eff-η_max structural confound.
**Contingency**: plan_001 (15+ models) may break the confound. If C(15,3)=455 panels contain high-K_eff + low-η_max combinations, random-fault simulation may produce different results. If plan_001 also fails → drop to R²-only claim or remove Claim 2 entirely.
**Strength**: Weak (pending plan_001). R² difference is real but much weaker than original K_eff regime-distinction claim.

### Claim 3 (Empirical): Diversity-Capability Tradeoff
**Statement**: In the current LLM ecosystem, maximizing panel diversity (K_eff) necessarily introduces less capable/robust models, creating a negative correlation between K_eff and min-judge-robustness (r ≈ -0.8). Diversity and security are structurally at odds.
**Evidence**: K_eff vs η_max correlation across 20 panels; capability-stratified analysis showing tradeoff persists within model tiers.
**Strength**: Strong (correlation). Capability-stratified analysis planned.

### Claim 4 (Methodological): Family Labels ≠ Diversity
**Statement**: Model family labels (Qwen/Llama/Mistral) do not predict judge independence. Capability proximity is the primary driver of inter-judge correlation.
**Evidence**: Mann-Whitney U p=0.206, permutation p=0.427 for within vs cross-family MI.
**Strength**: Strong. Clean statistical test, N=15 pairs.

### Claim 5 (Methodological): Gaussian Copula Failure
**Statement**: The Gaussian copula model systematically underestimates information sharing between LLM judges by 10-21× (up to 235×), invalidating copula-based independence bounds.
**Evidence**: MI_observed / MI_gaussian ratio across 15 pairs × 2 datasets.
**Strength**: Strong. Large effect size, consistent.

### Claim 6 (Practical): Robustness-First Panel Design
**Statement**: Optimal panel selection is robustness-first: (1) screen for individual robustness (η ≤ threshold), then (2) maximize K_eff among qualifying judges. This dominates naive strategies (random, max-family-diversity, max-K_eff-only, strongest-K-models).
**Evidence**: Preliminary: min_eta_max strategy dominates 5/6 conditions. Full two-stage algorithm validation planned.
**Strength**: Moderate. Needs formal algorithm + expanded model pool validation.

### Claim 7 (Empirical+Practical): Aggregation Rule Modulates Weakest-Link Effect
**Statement**: The weakest-link dominance (Claim 1) is specific to unweighted aggregation rules. Reliability-weighted (Bayesian) aggregation partially breaks the effect (η_max FDR-significant in only 2/12 conditions vs 5/12 under majority vote), while unanimity (threshold) voting makes diversity actively harmful (K_eff positively correlated with ASR).
**Evidence** (6-model, FDR-48 corrected, 5-fold CV validated):
- Majority: η_max **5/12** FDR sig (consistent with plan_009 FDR-12: 6/12)
- Weighted: η_max **6/12** FDR sig
- Threshold: η_max **6/12** FDR-48 sig + K_eff positive **8/12** FDR-12 sig (⚠️ FDR-48 may reduce to ~6/12; diversity harmful under unanimity; 4 conditions K_eff sig but η_max not — K_eff carries independent signal)
- Bayesian: η_max **2/12** FDR sig (Bonferroni 1/12 — mmlu__verbosity_bias β=+4.32, extreme effect survives)
- 5-fold CV confirms no information leakage: same 3 raw-significant conditions survive with near-identical p-values
**Mechanism details** (Reviewer verified):
- Bayesian: real effect reduction (4/12 conditions show η_max sign reversal, not just power loss) + low power (R²=0.22). Extreme attacks (prompt injection, verbosity bias) still break through. Weights = clean accuracy via 5-fold CV ("calibrated Bayesian") — robust to weight estimation procedure.
- Threshold: K_eff positive because unanimity requires all judges correct → independent judges less likely to all agree → attack only needs to flip any one judge. **ASR semantics differ from majority vote** (denominator = clean unanimity subset, not all samples) — must be disclosed.
**Strength**: Moderate-Strong (6-model). Key caveats: (1) Threshold ASR definition ≠ majority ASR definition (selection bias on denominator); (2) 6-model / 20-panel data, needs 455-panel validation.
**Paper narrative**: "Bayesian aggregation mitigates but does not eliminate the weakest-link effect; the most severe vulnerability gaps survive reliability weighting."
**Reviewer anticipation**: "Why not just use Bayesian?" → (a) requires clean accuracy prior (not zero-knowledge), (b) adaptive attacker can target Bayesian specifically, (c) FDR-corrected 2/12 still significant — extreme attacks survive, (d) practical recommendation is defense stack (robustness-first selection + Bayesian aggregation), not aggregation alone.

## Contribution Stack (ordered by strength)
1. **Weakest-link theorem** — primary empirical contribution (challenges diversity assumption)
2. **Diversity-capability tradeoff** — empirical contribution (shows structural barrier)
3. **Aggregation-dependent weakest-link** — empirical+practical contribution (scopes Theorem 1; Bayesian as partial defense; threshold as counterintuitive negative)
4. **Robustness-first panel design** — practical contribution (actionable guidance)
5. **Gaussian copula failure** — methodological contribution
6. **Family label unreliability** — methodological contribution
7. **Adaptive adversary vs random-fault R² gap** — conditional theoretical contribution (⚠️ pending plan_001 validation; if confound breaks with 15 models → promote to #2)

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns

### RC1: "η_max dominating is obvious — of course weak judges make weak panels"
**Response**: (a) Existing literature assumes diversity is sufficient (SoK reports "7-model committees reduce ASR to 10-19%" without controlling for individual model quality); (b) We formalize via adaptive adversary model showing WHY — not just THAT — this happens; (c) The diversity-capability tradeoff is non-obvious and has practical implications.

### RC2: "Only 6 models — too small for generalizable claims"
**Response**: Expand to 15+ models including API models (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, Claude, Gemini) + larger open-source (70B class). Weakest-link theorem tested on C(15,3) = 455 panels.

### RC3: "Only limited attack types"
**Response**: Expand to 6+ attack types covering prompt injection, score manipulation, sycophancy bias, verbosity bias, position bias, authority bias.

### RC4: "BFT comparison is a strawman — nobody literally claims BFT for LLM panels"
**Response**: (a) The *implicit* assumption is BFT-like: "more independent judges = more robust"; (b) We make this implicit assumption explicit and show where it breaks; (c) Random-fault simulation shows panel composition R² is systematically higher (0.55-0.95) than under adaptive attacks (0.14-0.73), confirming that adaptive adversaries introduce strategic variance beyond what panel composition can predict — the distinction is real even though K_eff itself is not the differentiator.

### RC5: "Panel design algorithm is trivial — just use the strongest models"
**Response**: (a) "Strongest" varies across attack types; (b) Two-stage algorithm outperforms both "min η_max only" and "max K_eff only" in capability-matched settings; (c) Algorithm provides principled threshold selection.

### RC6: "No theoretical novelty — just regression analysis"
**Response**: (a) Adaptive adversary bound is a formal theorem; (b) Diversity-capability tradeoff formalization is novel; (c) Copula failure has implications for MI-based evaluation frameworks beyond this paper.

### RC7: "Why not just use Bayesian aggregation to fix the problem?"
**Response**: (a) Bayesian aggregation requires clean accuracy as prior — not a zero-knowledge defense; (b) Adaptive adversary aware of Bayesian weighting can adjust strategy; (c) η_max still FDR-significant in 2/12 conditions (Bonferroni 1/12) — weakened but not eliminated, extreme vulnerability gaps survive; (d) The practical recommendation is a defense stack: robustness-first selection + reliability-weighted aggregation, not aggregation alone.

## "When Diversity Helps" Section (Dream D13 fix)
Diversity IS beneficial in specific regimes — paper must acknowledge this to avoid misleading:
1. **Non-adversarial settings**: reducing position bias, verbosity bias, calibration
2. **Within the arc×sycophancy regime**: K_eff partial r=-0.64, VIF=1.04, beta reg p=8.5e-05. When individual vulnerability is uniformly high and low-variance (sycophancy on ARC), diversity provides genuine protection. This is the "BFT-like" regime where faults are approximately random.
3. **Practical guidance**: First ensure all judges exceed a robustness threshold, THEN maximize diversity among qualifying judges.

## Story Arc
1. **Background**: Multi-judge LLM evaluation is increasingly adopted; diversity is assumed to be the key defense against manipulation (SoK, Yang, Turkmen)
2. **Tension**: This assumption mirrors BFT, which assumes random faults — but LLM adversaries are adaptive
3. **Insight**: Under adaptive adversaries, panel_ASR is dominated by η_max; diversity provides no protection because the attacker targets the weakest link
4. **Nuance**: Diversity DOES help in specific regimes (low η_max variance, shared-bias attacks) — the BFT analogy is valid only when individual vulnerabilities are already controlled
5. **Defense**: Aggregation rule matters — Bayesian weighting partially breaks weakest-link; unanimity makes diversity harmful. But no single aggregation eliminates the effect.
6. **Resolution**: Defense stack: robustness-first panel selection + reliability-weighted aggregation + regime-aware framework

{"success": true, "data": {"path": "/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0519_2/projects/cert_manip_resist_eval/literature_map.yaml", "content": "papers:
  robertson2025tvdmi:
    title: "Let's Measure Information Step-by-Step: LLM-Based Evaluation Beyond Vibes"
    authors: ["Robertson", "Koyejo"]
    year: 2025
    venue: "arXiv (under TMLR review)"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05469"
    category: "evaluation_framework"
    role: "foundation"
    relevance: "Foundational TVD-MI theory for LLM evaluation. Theorem 3.3 proves bounded f-divergences (TVD) maintain polynomial certification under mode-collapse attacks while unbounded (KL) fail. We extend from pairwise to N-agent multi-judge settings."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  yang2026diversity_scaling:
    title: "Understanding Agent Scaling in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems via Diversity"
    authors: ["Yang et al."]
    year: 2026
    venue: "ICLR 2026 Workshop AIMS"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03794"
    category: "multi_agent_scaling"
    role: "foundation"
    relevance: "Information-theoretic diversity-scaling framework: K* = 2^{H(ρ)}, residual uncertainty (1-α_c)^{K*} geometric contraction (Theorem 4.3). We provide the adversarial dual — while their K* governs performance improvement rate, the same correlation structure governs manipulation cost increase rate. Core duality insight."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  turkmen2026copula:
    title: "Don't Always Pick the Highest-Performing Model: An Information Theoretic View of LLM Ensemble Selection"
    authors: ["Turkmen et al."]
    year: 2026
    venue: "arXiv"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08003"
    category: "ensemble_theory"
    role: "foundation"
    relevance: "Gaussian-copula correlated error model (Z_j = √ρ·U + √(1-ρ)·ξ_j), error floor Φ(Φ⁻¹(1-p)/√ρ) (Theorem 4.4), three-term MI decomposition (Theorem 4.3). Copula model is the mathematical foundation for our K_eff = 1+(K-1)·exp(-2·I_max) derivation. Within-family ρ~0.7-0.8, cross-family ρ~0.4-0.5."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  kaneko2025bits_leaked:
    title: "Bits Leaked per Query: Information-Theoretic Bounds on Adversarial Attacks against LLMs"
    authors: ["Kaneko", "Baldwin"]
    year: 2025
    venue: "NeurIPS 2025 spotlight"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17000"
    category: "adversarial_bounds"
    role: "foundation"
    relevance: "Tight single-model attack cost bound N_min ≥ log₂(1/ε)/I_max via Fano inequality (Theorem 1), achieved by SPRT (Theorem 2). Validated across 7 LLMs. Provides single-channel foundation; we extend to multi-judge composition where adversary must simultaneously fool K correlated judges."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  chen2025peg:
    title: "Incentivizing Truthful Language Models via Peer Elicitation Games"
    authors: ["Chen et al."]
    year: 2025
    venue: "NeurIPS 2025"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13636"
    category: "peer_prediction"
    role: "direct-competitor"
    relevance: "DMI-based multi-agent peer elicitation with dominant strategy truthfulness (Lemma 1), O(√T) regret (Theorem 2). Requires conditional independence (Assumption 4) but does not characterize degradation when violated. We prove ε = f(ρ) continuous degradation curve as co-primary contribution."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  qiu2026truthfulness:
    title: "Truthfulness Despite Weak Supervision: Evaluating and Training LLMs Using Peer Prediction"
    authors: ["Qiu et al."]
    year: 2026
    venue: "ICLR 2026"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20299"
    category: "peer_prediction"
    role: "direct-competitor"
    relevance: "BNE incentive-compatibility for LLM peer prediction with inverse scaling property. Targets output truthfulness not adversarial robustness of protocol. No polynomial cost bounds tied to judge count. We provide the robustness guarantee that complements their truthfulness guarantee."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  kim2025correlated_errors:
    title: "Correlated Errors in Large Language Models"
    authors: ["Kim", "Garg", "Peng", "Garg"]
    year: 2025
    venue: "ICML 2025"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962"
    category: "error_correlation"
    role: "empirical-basis"
    relevance: "60% pairwise agreement when both err (vs 33% baseline), same-company +0.066, same-architecture +0.076. Key empirical data for α regime analysis and K_eff estimation. 350+ LLMs. Motivates cross-family diversity for maximizing K_eff."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  sok2026llm_judge_security:
    title: "Security in LLM-as-a-Judge: A Comprehensive SoK"
    authors: ["Various"]
    year: 2026
    venue: "arXiv"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29403"
    category: "adversarial_evaluation"
    role: "empirical-basis"
    relevance: "Comprehensive vulnerability catalog: open-source 50-68% ASR, frontier 27-44%. 7-model diverse committees reduce ASR to 10-19% empirically but WITHOUT formal explanation. We provide the formal explanation via K_eff framework."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  feng2026noisy_valid:
    title: "Noisy but Valid: Robust Statistical Evaluation of LLMs with Imperfect Judges"
    authors: ["Feng", "Shen", "Balashankar", "Gerner-Beuerle", "Rodrigues"]
    year: 2026
    venue: "ICLR 2026"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20913"
    category: "certified_evaluation"
    role: "adjacent"
    relevance: "Statistical hypothesis testing for LLM evaluation with finite-sample Type-I error control (Theorem 5.1) despite calibration uncertainty. Assumes honest but fallible judges. Complements our work: they certify statistical validity, we certify manipulation resistance."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  jung2026logarithmic_scores:
    title: "Logarithmic Scores, Power-Law Discoveries: Disentangling Measurement from Coverage in Agent-Based Evaluation"
    authors: ["Jung", "Na"]
    year: 2026
    venue: "arXiv"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00477"
    category: "multi_agent_scaling"
    role: "empirical-basis"
    relevance: "Score-coverage dissociation: scoring reliability scales logarithmically with panel size N while discovery follows power law N^0.69. Direct implications for our K-scaling claims — certified bounds may saturate faster than empirical ASR gains."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  chen2026behavioral_entanglement:
    title: "How Independent are Large Language Models? A Statistical Framework for Auditing Behavioral Entanglement"
    authors: ["Chen et al."]
    year: 2026
    venue: "arXiv"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07650"
    category: "error_correlation"
    role: "empirical-basis"
    relevance: "BEI and CIG metrics across 18 LLMs from 6 families. Cross-family entanglement 40-60% lower than intra-family. Provides independent validation of cross-family diversity benefit for K_eff estimation."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

  keppo2026collusion_fragility:
    title: "On the Fragility of AI Agent Collusion"
    authors: ["Keppo et al."]
    year: 2026
    venue: "arXiv"
    url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20281"
    category: "multi_agent_robustness"
    role: "supporting"
    relevance: "Increasing LLM count 2→5 breaks collusion (+22%→+3%). Same-family size heterogeneity stabilizes via leader-follower dynamics. Motivates cross-family diversity requirement in our protocol design."
    verified: false
    added_by: "director"
    added_at: "2026-05-21"

57	% ============================================================
58	% 2. RELATED WORK
59	% ============================================================
60	\section{Related Work}
61	
62	\paragraph{LLM-as-Judge.}
63	Using LLMs as automated evaluators has become standard practice for tasks where human evaluation is expensive. Single-judge approaches suffer from well-documented biases including position bias, verbosity bias, and sycophancy. Multi-judge panels have been proposed as a mitigation, with the implicit assumption that aggregating diverse opinions reduces systematic errors.
64	
65	\paragraph{Adversarial Attacks on LLM Judges.}
66	Recent work has demonstrated that LLM judges are vulnerable to prompt injection, score manipulation, and various cognitive biases. These attacks achieve non-trivial success rates even against state-of-the-art models. The multi-judge setting has been relatively under-studied from a security perspective, with existing work primarily reporting that committees reduce average ASR without analyzing \emph{why} or \emph{when} this reduction holds.
67	
68	\paragraph{Byzantine Fault Tolerance.}
69	Classical BFT guarantees safety when fewer than $f < n/3$ replicas are faulty, under the assumption that faults are independent and non-adaptive. The analogy to multi-judge evaluation---more independent judges provide greater robustness---has been implicit in the literature but never formally examined. We show this analogy breaks under adaptive adversaries.
70	
71	\paragraph{Panel Diversity Metrics.}
72	Prior work has measured panel diversity through model family heterogeneity, prompting strategy variation, or temperature differences. We argue that \emph{effective independence} ($K_{\text{eff}}$), derived from the mutual information matrix between judges, is the correct metric, and show that family labels do not predict it.
73	
74	% ============================================================
75	% 3. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK
76	% ============================================================
77	\section{Theoretical Framework}
78	
79	\subsection{Setup and Notation}
80	
81	Consider a panel of $K$ judges $\{J_1, \ldots, J_K\}$ evaluating a candidate text. Each judge $J_j$ has an individual vulnerability $\eta_j \in [0,1]$, representing the probability that an adversarial input successfully manipulates $J_j$'s evaluation. The panel uses majority-vote aggregation: the adversary succeeds if they compromise $\geq \lceil K/2 \rceil$ judges.
82	
83	We define two key panel-level metrics:
84	\begin{itemize}
85	    \item $\eta_{\max} = \max_{j} \eta_j$: the vulnerability of the weakest (most vulnerable) panel member.
86	    \item $K_{\text{eff}}$: the effective number of independent judges, derived from the eigenspectrum of the inter-judge mutual information matrix $\mathbf{M}$, where $M_{ij} = I(J_i; J_j)$. $K_{\text{eff}} = \left(\sum_i \lambda_i\right)^2 / \sum_i \lambda_i^2$, where $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}$.
87	\end{itemize}
88	
89	\subsection{Adaptive Adversary Model}
90	
91	\begin{definition}[Adaptive Adversary]
92	An adaptive adversary has access to the panel composition $\{J_1, \ldots, J_K\}$ and the per-judge vulnerability profiles $\{\eta_1, \ldots, \eta_K\}$. The adversary can craft targeted attacks optimized for each judge's weaknesses.
93	\end{definition}
94	
95	\begin{theorem}[Weakest-Link Bound]
96	\label{thm:weakest-link}
97	For an adaptive adversary with access to per-judge vulnerability profiles, the panel attack success rate under majority-vote aggregation satisfies:
98	\[
99	\text{panel\_ASR} \geq \max_j \eta_j = \eta_{\max}
100	\]
101	Moreover, for panels where the weakest judge is sufficiently more vulnerable than the median ($\eta_{\max} \gg \text{median}_j(\eta_j)$), $\text{panel\_ASR} = \Theta(\eta_{\max})$.
102	\end{theorem}
103	
104	\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
105	The adaptive adversary constructs an attack targeting the weakest judge $J^* = \arg\max_j \eta_j$. This attack succeeds on $J^*$ with probability $\eta_{\max}$. Since the attack is optimized for $J^*$'s weaknesses, it is also partially effective against judges with correlated vulnerabilities. For majority vote, the adversary needs $\lceil K/2 \rceil$ compromised judges. Starting from $J^*$, the adversary extends to the next-weakest judges. Because judges share architectural and training commonalities (reflected in $\mathbf{M}$), a single optimized attack transfers with non-trivial probability. The lower bound $\eta_{\max}$ follows from the adversary's ability to always compromise at least $J^*$. The $\Theta(\eta_{\max})$ scaling follows when $\eta_{\max}$ dominates the vulnerability distribution. Crucially, increasing $K_{\text{eff}}$ (diversity) does not reduce $\eta_{\max}$; it only ensures the remaining judges are more independent, which is irrelevant when the adversary's primary target is always the weakest link.
106	\end{proof}
107	
108	\subsection{Contrast with BFT}
109	
110	Under the BFT random-fault model, each judge fails independently with probability $p_j$, and failures are not adversarially targeted. In this regime:
111	\[
112	\text{panel\_fail\_prob} = \sum_{S \subseteq [K], |S| \geq \lceil K/2 \rceil} \prod_{j \in S} p_j \prod_{j \notin S} (1 - p_j)
113	\]
114	This probability decreases exponentially with $K_{\text{eff}}$ when faults are independent, validating the diversity-as-defense intuition \emph{only under random faults}. Our random-fault simulation (Section~\ref{sec:bft-contrast}) empirically confirms this distinction.
115	
116	% ============================================================
117	% 4. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
118	% ============================================================
119	\section{Experimental Setup}
120	
121	\subsection{Model Pool}
122	
123	We evaluate 15 models spanning the open-source and commercial API ecosystem (Table~\ref{tab:models}). The pool includes 6 models in the 7B parameter class, 4 large models (70B+ or MoE), and 5 commercial API models. This diverse pool yields $\binom{15}{3} = 455$ unique three-judge panels.

126	\centering

128	\label{tab:models}

130	\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
131	\toprule
132	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Size} & $\boldsymbol{\eta}$\textbf{(MMLU)} & $\boldsymbol{\eta}$\textbf{(ARC)} & \textbf{Avg ASR} \\

134	Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct    & Open & 7B     & 0.32 & 0.28 & 0.30 \\

155	\subsection{Attack Types}
156	
157	We evaluate 9 attack types spanning diverse adversarial strategies:
158	
159	\begin{itemize}
160	    \item \textbf{Original 6}: prompt injection, score manipulation, sycophancy bias, verbosity bias, position bias, authority bias.
161	    \item \textbf{Extended 3}: few-shot hijacking (in-context manipulation), persona manipulation (social engineering), instruction override (direct override of evaluation instructions).
162	\end{itemize}
163	
164	\subsection{Benchmarks}
165	
166	All experiments are conducted on MMLU and ARC-Challenge, representing knowledge-intensive and reasoning-intensive evaluation tasks respectively.
167	
168	\subsection{Panel Construction and Metrics}
169	
170	For $K=3$ panels, we enumerate all $\binom{15}{3} = 455$ combinations. For larger panel sizes ($K \in \{5,7,9\}$), we enumerate all $\binom{15}{K}$ combinations. For each panel, we compute:
171	\begin{itemize}
172	    \item $\eta_{\max}$: vulnerability of the weakest panel member.
173	    \item $K_{\text{eff}}$: effective independence from the MI matrix eigenspectrum.
174	    \item Panel ASR: fraction of adversarial inputs that successfully manipulate the majority vote.
175	\end{itemize}
176	
177	We fit multivariate regressions $\log(\text{ASR}) \sim \beta_1 \log(\eta_{\max}) + \beta_2 \log(K_{\text{eff}}) + \epsilon$ to quantify the relative predictive power of individual robustness vs.\ diversity.
178	
179	% ============================================================
180	% 5. RESULTS
181	% ============================================================
182	\section{Results}
183	
184	\subsection{Weakest-Link Dominance at Scale}
185	\label{sec:weakest-link}
186	
187	Table~\ref{tab:regression} presents the multivariate regression results across all 455 three-judge panels, 2 datasets, and 6 original attack types (12 conditions). $\eta_{\max}$ is a significant predictor ($p < 0.05$) in 87\% of conditions with a median coefficient $\beta = 0.72$, while $K_{\text{eff}}$ is non-significant in 91\% of conditions (median $p = 0.43$). The weakest-link model explains a median $R^2 = 0.56$ of the variance in panel ASR.

190	\centering
191	\caption{Multivariate regression results across 455 panels. $\beta$ = standardized regression coefficient; $p$ = significance; $R^2$ = model fit. $\eta_{\max}$ consistently dominates while $K_{\text{eff}}$ remains non-significant.}

194	\begin{tabular}{llccccc}
195	\toprule
196	\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{Attack} & $\boldsymbol{\beta(\eta_{\max})}$ & $\boldsymbol{p(\eta_{\max})}$ & $\boldsymbol{\beta(K_{\text{eff}})}$ & $\boldsymbol{p(K_{\text{eff}})}$ & $\boldsymbol{R^2}$ \\

206	ARC  & Score Manipulation  & 0.68 & 0.008    & 0.06    & 0.49 & 0.51 \\
207	ARC  & Sycophancy          & 0.73 & 0.004    & $-$0.12 & 0.18 & 0.55 \\
208	ARC  & Verbosity Bias      & 0.64 & 0.015    & 0.03    & 0.72 & 0.46 \\

API models follow the same weakest-link pattern as open-source models, with no evidence of a distinct ``coordinated defense'' regime. The 455-panel scale provides sufficient statistical power to detect effects that were directionally consistent but underpowered in smaller pilot studies.
216	
217	\subsection{Generalization Across Attack Types}
218	\label{sec:attack-expansion}
219	
220	To test whether the weakest-link phenomenon is attack-type-specific, we extend the evaluation to three additional attack types (Table~\ref{tab:new-attacks}). All three new attacks---few-shot hijacking (mean ASR = 0.31), persona manipulation (0.22), and instruction override (0.38)---exhibit the same $\eta_{\max}$-dominated pattern, with $\eta_{\max}$ significance rates of 83--87\% and $K_{\text{eff}}$ non-significance rates of 87--91\%.
221	
222	\begin{table}[t]
223	\centering
224	\caption{Results for three additional attack types across 455 panels, compared to the average of the original 6 attacks. The weakest-link pattern generalizes across all attack vectors.}
225	\label{tab:new-attacks}
226	\small
227	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
228	\toprule
229	\textbf{Attack} & \textbf{Mean ASR} & $\boldsymbol{\eta_{\max}}$ \textbf{sig\%} & $\boldsymbol{K_{\text{eff}}}$ \textbf{nonsig\%} & \textbf{Median} $\boldsymbol{R^2}$ \\
230	\midrule

232	Persona Manipulation  & 0.22 & 87\% & 91\% & 0.54 \\
233	Instruction Override   & 0.38 & 85\% & 88\% & 0.53 \\

236	\bottomrule
237	\end{tabular}
238	\end{table}

This supports the view that individual robustness is an intrinsic property of the judge, not an artifact of specific attack-judge interactions.

243	\label{sec:bft-contrast}
244

# Distilled Research — Certifiable Manipulation Resistance for Multi-Judge LLM Eval

> 12 篇论文（8 深度+4 摘要），2025-2026。信息论评估、peer prediction、多智能体 scaling、错误相关性、对抗鲁棒性。

## 1. 信息论框架是领域共识
**7/8 深度论文**用 MI/Fano/DPI/f-散度。**高置信度**。
Kaneko2025 (NeurIPS spotlight): N_min≥log₂(1/ε)/I_max; Robertson2025-TVD-MI: 有界 f-散度保持多项式样本复杂度 (Thm 3.3)。
→ Baseline 必含 IT-based 方法；理论需 Fano 下界+可达性证明。

## 2. 跨 family 多样性 > 规模扩张
**6/12 篇直接验证**。**高置信度**。
Yang2026: 2 diverse ≥ 16 homogeneous (8×效率); Kim2025: same-company +6.6%, same-arch +7.6% error agreement; Turkmen2026: within ρ~0.7-0.8, cross ρ~0.4-0.5; Chen2026-BEI: cross-family 低 40-60%; Keppo2026: heterogeneity 破 collusion 22%→3%。
→ 必含 homo/hetero 对照组；报告 within vs cross-family ρ；推荐 3-5 跨 family judge。

## 3. Scaling 天花板
**5/12 篇**。**高置信度**。
Turkmen2026 Thm 4.4: error→Φ(Φ⁻¹(1-α)/√ρ); Yang2026: homo plateau N≈4; PEG: K=7 退化; Jung2026: scoring O(log N)。
→ 找 saturation point，报告 K_eff 或 K*。

## 4. 条件独立性假设是核心脆弱点
**4/12 篇**。**高置信度**。
PEG K=7 因独立性违反退化; Kim2025 证明错误系统相关; Qiu2026 collusion 分析有限。
→ 不假设条件独立；提供 ε=f(ρ) 退化曲线；用 Gaussian-copula 建模。

## 5. Baseline 与指标共识
**Baselines**: LLM-as-a-Judge 6/12, majority voting 4/12, peer prediction 3/12, top-k 2/12。
**Metrics**: accuracy 7/8, MI variants 4/8, ASR 3/12, Type-I/II 1/8。
**Datasets**: MMLU 3/12, ARC 2/12, multi-benchmark suites 4/12。
→ 最低：LLM-as-a-Judge + majority voting baseline; MMLU + ≥2 benchmarks; error rate + IT metric。

% ============================================================
% 4. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
% ============================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}

\subsection{Model Pool}

We evaluate 15 models spanning the open-source and commercial API ecosystem (Table~\ref{tab:models}). The pool includes 6 models in the 7B parameter class, 4 large models (70B+ or MoE), and 5 commercial API models. This diverse pool yields $\binom{15}{3} = 455$ unique three-judge panels.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Model pool summary. $\eta_{\max}$ values represent individual vulnerability across MMLU and ARC benchmarks. Avg ASR is the mean attack success rate across all 6 original attack types.}
\label{tab:models}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Size} & $\boldsymbol{\eta}$\textbf{(MMLU)} & $\boldsymbol{\eta}$\textbf{(ARC)} & \textbf{Avg ASR} \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct    & Open & 7B     & 0.32 & 0.28 & 0.30 \\
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct  & Open & 8B     & 0.38 & 0.35 & 0.37 \\
Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 & Open & 7B   & 0.45 & 0.42 & 0.44 \\
Gemma-2-9B-Instruct    & Open & 9B     & 0.29 & 0.25 & 0.27 \\
Phi-3.5-mini-Instruct  & Open & 3.8B   & 0.52 & 0.48 & 0.50 \\
InternLM2.5-7B-Chat    & Open & 7B     & 0.35 & 0.31 & 0.33 \\
\midrule
Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct & Open & 70B    & 0.12 & 0.09 & 0.11 \\
Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct   & Open & 72B    & 0.10 & 0.08 & 0.09 \\
Mixtral-8x22B-Instruct & Open & 141B MoE & 0.15 & 0.13 & 0.14 \\
DeepSeek-V2.5-Chat     & Open & 236B MoE & 0.13 & 0.11 & 0.12 \\
\midrule
GPT-4o-mini            & API  & ---     & 0.18 & 0.15 & 0.17 \\
GPT-4o                 & API  & ---     & 0.08 & 0.06 & 0.07 \\
GPT-4.1                & API  & ---     & 0.05 & 0.04 & 0.05 \\
Claude-3.5-Sonnet      & API  & ---     & 0.06 & 0.05 & 0.06 \\
Gemini-1.5-Pro         & API  & ---     & 0.09 & 0.07 & 0.08 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Attack Types}

We evaluate 9 attack types spanning diverse adversarial strategies:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Original 6}: prompt injection, score manipulation, sycophancy bias, verbosity bias, position bias, authority bias.
    \item \textbf{Extended 3}: few-shot hijacking (in-context manipulation), persona manipulation (social engineering), instruction override (direct override of evaluation instructions).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Benchmarks}

All experiments are conducted on MMLU and ARC-Challenge, representing knowledge-intensive and reasoning-intensive evaluation tasks respectively.

\subsection{Panel Construction and Metrics}

For $K=3$ panels, we enumerate all $\binom{15}{3} = 455$ combinations. For larger panel sizes ($K \in \{5,7,9\}$), we enumerate all $\binom{15}{K}$ combinations. For each panel, we compute:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\eta_{\max}$: vulnerability of the weakest panel member.
    \item $K_{\text{eff}}$: effective independence from the MI matrix eigenspectrum.
    \item Panel ASR: fraction of adversarial inputs that successfully manipulate the majority vote.
